text: In the tenth year of the war, everything comes down to two men. Outside the walls of Troy, Achilles and Hector will meet at last, and only one of them will walk away.
The Trojan army has fled in terror behind the gates. One man stays outside — Hector, their greatest warrior, the shield of his city, waiting alone.
From the high walls his old father Priam and his mother Hecuba cry out, begging him to come inside. But Hector will not run from this fight.
Then Achilles comes on, terrible in his armor, his spear-point gleaming like a star in the dark. Homer calls it the fairest star of all: Ἕσπερος, ὃς κάλλιστος ἐν οὐρανῷ ἵσταται ἀστήρ.
And at that sight, even Hector's courage breaks. Fear takes him, and he runs. Three times the two of them race around the walls of Troy.
High on Olympus, Zeus lifts his golden scales and weighs two fates of death, one for each man. The doom of Hector sinks down toward the house of Hades.
Then the goddess Athena deceives him. Disguised as his own brother, she swears to stand at his side — and then she vanishes. Hector must face Achilles alone.
They hurl their spears. But Achilles knows the armor stripped from Patroclus, and he knows the one place the throat is left bare. There he drives the bronze home.
Hector falls. And Homer gives us one of the most famous lines in all of Greek: ψυχὴ δ᾽ ἐκ ῥεθέων πταμένη Ἄϊδόσδε βεβήκει — his soul, flying from his limbs, went down to the house of Hades.
This is the death of Hector, the bravest defender of Troy, in Book Twenty-Two of Homer's Iliad. With his fall, the doom of the great city itself draws near.
